http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/24/us-st.text: The United States military said on Monday it carried out a strike on an alleged drug trafficking boat in the Pacific Ocean, killing two people.US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said in a post on X that the strike, which took place on Sunday, targeted a vessel "operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific.""Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking," it added."This operation is a clear and decisive reminder that SOUTHCOM is taking the fight directly to the cartels," SOUTHCOM said.Grainy black-and-white video footage accompanying the post showed a boat moving through the water before a large explosion.The US military launched operation "Southern Spear" in early September, with President Donald Trump arguing Washington is effectively at war with drug cartels operating out of Latin America.Since then, more than 200 people have been killed in strikes in the Eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea, according to a tally by the AFP news agency.Trump's administration has not provided definitive evidence that the vessels it has been striking are involved in drug trafficking.Legal experts and rights groups say the strikes could amount to extrajudicial killings.

Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty Images Houthis Houthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coast Iran and its proxies move closer to full control of two shipping chokepoints as regional conflict widens Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Thu 10 Sep 2026 07.39 EDT Last modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 11.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Yemen’s Houthi rebels are making a concerted drive to take full control of the country’s Red Sea coast, claiming control of the key port of Mocha, in the most serious wave of fighting with the Saudi-backed government in years. Seizure of the coast would be a strategic disaster for Saudi Arabia and the US, taking Iran and its proxies closer to full control of two chokepoints for western shipping on opposite sides of the Arabian peninsula: the Bab al-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea and the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. Observers have said a reduction in hostilities – the most intense since the UN-sponsored ceasefire of April 2022 put an end to major military exchanges – now seems unlikely in what is seen as an attempt by the Houthis to open a second front in the Iran-US war, alongside the battle for control of Hormuz. The Royal United Services Institute ( Rusi), a London-based defence and security thinktank, said the situation in Yemen was spiralling out of control, adding that the UN-recognised Yemeni government was opening new fronts against the Houthis in the hope it could put more pressure on the rebels than they could withstand. View image in fullscreen A screengrab from video footage released by Saudi-backed forces shows a rocket being fired during fighting in Taiz province. Photograph: Yemen National Resistance Forces/AFP/Getty Images The fighting has also raised questions about whether Saudi Arabia, which on Thursday launched as many as 40 airstrikes on Houthi targets, will activate the Mecca defence agreement and ask its co-signatories, Pakistan and Turkey, to send forces. The pact is designed to be defensive in nature and believed unlikely to apply to Saudi military activities in Yemen. A map showing the area of Yemen controlled by Houthi rebels By taking control of more of the Red Sea coast south of the port of Hodeidah, the Houthis’ aim is to put pressure on Saudi Arabia and the US to agree a deal that lifts the US blockade on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf. Donald Trump on Wednesday acknowledged he did not expect the war with Iran to end before the US midterm elections at the start of November. The latest phase in the escalation began when Houthis attacked energy installations and southern cities in Saudi Arabia using drones and ballistic missiles. In response, the kingdom’s military forces launched at least 15 strikes between 3 and 7 September. View image in fullscreen The aftermath of Houthi strikes on Mocha last month. The rebel group claims it now controls the port. Photograph: Al Joumhouriya TV/Reuters The conflict data monitor Acled estimated there were 276 fatalities over the five-day period alone. The fighting has continued, with the Houthis claiming control of Mocha in Taiz province, as well as the inland city of Hays and the Khalid ibn al-Walid camp, the largest military base in the region. One Houthi-linked estimate suggested rebel forces had gained control of more than 2,320 sq miles (6,000 sq km) of land. The commander of the Yemeni government forces, Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, admitted he had organised a strategic retreat south of Mocha in order to regroup in a secure location. “The armed forces in the western coast paid a heavy price – martyrs and wounded – over the past days as they confronted the Houthi attack planned by Iran, and supported by it,” he said. View image in fullscreen A satellite image shows smoke billowing from an Aramco oil depot near the Saudi city of Abha after a Houthi attack. Photograph: Planet Labs/AFP/Getty Images Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, continues to take advantage of its air superiority to attack Houthi positions, though government sources acknowledged the rebels’ ground advances along the coast and their missile strikes on the strategic Red Sea islands of Zuqar and Hanish. The clashes have ranged across Yemen, including Ad Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwah, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, and Taiz. In the initial days of the renewed conflict the Houthis found themselves being forced back in some areas as battles on multiple fronts overstretched their resources and fighter numbers. The Houthis will be hoping political divisions inside the Yemeni government, reflected in a lack of an integrated military, will slowly give them the upper hand. The United Arab Emirates, previously a powerful player in southern Yemen where it backed the separatist forces of the Southern Transitional Council, withdrew its financial and military support at the turn of the year. The southern forces have refused to fight outside their own region. View image in fullscreen A screengrab from video footage released by the Saudi-backed forces shows a fighter firing at Houthi rebels in Taiz province. Photograph: Yemen National Resistance Forces/AFP/Getty Images “ A reduction in hostilities anytime soon seems unlikely, as both sides continue to escalate with the goal of inflicting enough damage to the other side to force a compromise,” said Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst for Acled. “In terms of military capability, both sides are more equal compared to the immediate period prior to the 2022 ceasefire when the Houthis had the upper hand.” He added: “Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in Hodeidah and Taiz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-Yemen government have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab al-Mandab.” The fighting has contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80. View image in fullscreen A screengrab of video footage reportedly showing Houthi attacks on Saudi-backed forces in al-Jawf province. Photograph: Ansarullah Media Centre/AFP/Getty Images The escalantion to this week’s all-out violence has been a slow process. It began after a senior Houthi delegation from the group, which has long been in a complex alliance with Iran, flew to Tehran for the funeral of the Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei in July, returning in an Iranian plane that the Saudis refused to land in rebel-controlled Sana’a. The Saudis instead bombed the runway, leading the Houthis to announce a Red Sea naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in what the Yemeni rebels described as a blockade for a blockade. The 20 July announcement of the blockade was followed by a strike on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery on 25 July and on a tanker off Yanbu on 24 August. Saudi Arabia has become reliant on the Red Sea route for trade after Iran throttled shipping through the strait of Hormuz following US-Israeli attacks.
